html:
Paracas was a culture on the south coast of Peru, centred on the Paracas peninsula near Pisco, from about 800 to 100 BCE. People farmed the river valleys that cross the coastal desert and fished the rich sea.

It is famous for its textiles. In the 1920s the Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello found large cemeteries there, including hundreds of mummy bundles wrapped in many layers of cloth. The finest, the Paracas textiles, are embroidered mantles in bright colours with repeated figures of animals, gods and people.

Paracas people shaped the skulls of infants to make them long and practised trepanning, cutting holes in the skull, which some patients survived. Early Paracas art shows the influence of Chavín. Paracas grew directly into the Nazca culture, which kept many of its styles.
